section.title: The Arrest and the Trial before Pilate
section.sectionRationale: The Passion narrative begins. In the garden Jesus gives Himself up with sovereign calm, the arresting party falling back at His I am He, and He shields His disciples. He is taken before Annas and Caiaphas while Peter denies Him three times by a charcoal fire. Then, before Pilate, the true nature of His kingship comes to light: a kingdom not of this world, a King who came to bear witness to the truth, while the crowd chooses Barabbas.
section.thesis: Jesus goes to His arrest in full command, laying down His life freely and drinking the cup the Father has given, protecting His own even as Peter denies Him, and before Pilate He reveals Himself as a King whose kingdom is not of this world and who came to bear witness to the truth, though the world prefers a violent man to the King of truth.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the arrest in the garden and the I am He that fells the soldiers; Peter's first denial and Jesus before Annas; Peter's second and third denials; and the trial before Pilate, the kingdom not of this world, and the choice of Barabbas.

units.label: The arrest in the garden
units.note: I am He, and the cup the Father has given

verses.text: After Jesus had spoken these words, He went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley, where they entered a garden.
Now Judas His betrayer also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with His disciples.
So Judas brought a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees. They arrived at the garden carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons.
Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward and asked them, “Whom are you seeking?”
“Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. Jesus said, “{{egoeimi|I am He}}.” And Judas His betrayer was standing there with them.
When Jesus said, “I am He,” they drew back and fell to the ground.
So He asked them again, “Whom are you seeking?” “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered.
“I told you that I am He,” Jesus replied. “So if you are looking for Me, let these men go.”
This was to fulfill the word He had spoken: “I have not lost one of those You have given Me.”
Then Simon Peter drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
“Put your sword back in its sheath!” Jesus said to Peter. “Shall I not drink the {{poterion|cup}} the Father has given Me?”
Then the band of soldiers, with its commander and the officers of the Jews, arrested Jesus and bound Him.
They brought Him first to Annas, who was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year.
Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it would be better if one man died for the people.
Now Simon Peter and another disciple were following Jesus. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he also went with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest.
But Peter stood outside at the door. Then the disciple who was known to the high priest went out and spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in.
At this, the servant girl watching the door said to Peter, “Aren’t you also one of this man’s disciples?” “I am not,” he answered.
Because it was cold, the servants and officers were standing around a charcoal fire they had made to keep warm. And Peter was also standing with them, warming himself.
Meanwhile, the high priest questioned Jesus about His disciples and His teaching.
“I have spoken openly to the world,” Jesus answered. “I always taught in the synagogues and at the temple, where all the Jews come together. I said nothing in secret.
Why are you asking Me? Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said.”
When Jesus had said this, one of the officers standing nearby slapped Him in the face and said, “Is this how You answer the high priest?”
Jesus replied, “If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?”
Then Annas sent Him, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.
Simon Peter was still standing and warming himself. So they asked him, “Aren’t you also one of His disciples?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”
One of the high priest’s servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Didn’t I see you with Him in the garden?”
Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed.

units.label: Jesus before Pilate
units.note: My kingdom is not of this world

verses.text: Then they led Jesus away from Caiaphas into the Praetorium. By now it was early morning, and the Jews did not enter the Praetorium, to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover.
So Pilate went out to them and asked, “What accusation are you bringing against this man?”
“If He were not a criminal,” they replied, “we would not have handed Him over to you.”
“You take Him and judge Him by your own law,” Pilate told them. “We are not permitted to execute anyone,” the Jews replied.
This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to indicate the kind of death He was going to die.
Pilate went back into the Praetorium, summoned Jesus, and asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?”
“Are you saying this on your own,” Jesus asked, “or did others tell you about Me?”
“Am I a Jew?” Pilate replied. “Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?”
Jesus answered, “My {{basileia|kingdom}} is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews. But now My kingdom is not of this realm.”

“Then You are a king!” Pilate said. “You say that I am a king,” Jesus answered. “For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the {{aletheia|truth}}. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice.”
“What is truth?” Pilate asked. And having said this, he went out again to the Jews and told them, “I find no basis for a charge against Him.
But it is your custom that I release to you one prisoner at the Passover. So then, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”
“Not this man,” they shouted, “but Barabbas!” (Now Barabbas was an insurrectionist.)

egoeimi.gloss: I am, or I am He. When Jesus answers the arresting party with I am, they draw back and fall to the ground, a flash of the divine majesty behind the plain words, echoing the great I am. Even at His arrest, He is not seized against His will; He gives Himself up, and His word alone momentarily overpowers the armed band.

poterion.gloss: Cup. Jesus speaks of the cup the Father has given Him to drink, the Old Testament image of the cup of God's wrath against sin. To drink it is to bear that judgment in the place of His people. His willingness, shall I not drink the cup, shows His death is a chosen obedience, not a tragic accident.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, kingship, reign. Jesus tells Pilate His kingdom is not of this world, not sourced in or advanced by worldly power and violence, which is why His servants do not fight. It is no less real for that; He is truly a King, but His reign comes through truth and self-giving, not conquest, and it claims the allegiance of all who belong to the truth.

aletheia.gloss: Truth. Jesus says He was born and came into the world to bear witness to the truth, and that everyone who belongs to the truth hears His voice. Pilate's weary reply, what is truth, stands as the world's evasion before the One who is Himself the truth. Christ's kingship is exercised precisely by testifying to the truth.

basic.context: After the prayer, Jesus crosses into a garden, where Judas leads an armed party to arrest Him. Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; when He says I am He, they fall back to the ground. He gives Himself up but insists His disciples go free, and He stops Peter's sword, saying He must drink the cup the Father has given. Taken to Annas and Caiaphas, He is questioned and struck, while outside Peter denies knowing Him three times by a charcoal fire. Before Pilate, Jesus explains that His kingdom is not of this world and that He came to bear witness to the truth. Pilate finds no guilt, but the crowd demands Barabbas.
basic.hermeneutics: John shows Jesus in complete command even as He is arrested and tried; He is the one laying down His life, not a helpless victim. The key questions are, what kind of King is Jesus, and what is His kingdom. His kingdom is real but not of this world, not spread by force, and He reigns by bearing witness to the truth. Peter's denials, set against Jesus' bold confession, warn of the weakness of self-confidence. Pilate's what is truth captures the world's evasion before Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on a few words. Jesus' I am, ego eimi, momentarily fells the arresting party. He speaks of the poterion, the cup, of God's wrath He must drink. Before Pilate He declares His basileia, kingdom, is not of this world, and that He came to bear witness to the aletheia, the truth.
basic.typology: The garden of the arrest recalls the garden of Eden, where the first Adam fell; here the last Adam stands firm. The cup of wrath fulfills the prophetic image of the cup God's enemies must drink, now drunk by the Son in His people's place. Barabbas released while Jesus is condemned pictures the guilty going free because the innocent takes his place.
basic.christ: Christ is the sovereign, self-giving Lord who lays down His life, drinks the cup of wrath, protects His own, and reigns as the King of truth whose kingdom is not of this world. He stands innocent where Barabbas the guilty goes free.
basic.god: God the Father gives the cup, and the Son willingly drinks it, so that the whole Passion unfolds within the Father's purpose. God's kingdom advances not by the sword but by the truth and the cross.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 51 speaks of the cup of God's wrath. Luke 22 records the agony over the cup. John 6 and 17 promised Jesus would lose none. Revelation 19 shows Christ the King who conquers by truth.
basic.oneStory: In a garden the last Adam stands where the first fell, and He gives Himself to drink the cup of wrath His people deserved. Before earthly power He reveals a kingdom not of this world, ruled by truth, and the guilty Barabbas goes free while the innocent King is condemned, a picture of the whole gospel of substitution.

context.literary:
John 18 is told as a set of crossings. Jesus crosses the Kidron into a garden, verse 1. Peter is brought across the threshold of the high priest's courtyard, verses 15 and 16. Then the chief priests lead Jesus to the Praetorium but will not themselves go in, verse 28, and the rest of the chapter, running on into 19:16, has Pilate moving back and forth between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside. Many readers see seven scenes in that movement, alternating outside and inside: the accusation, the private interview about kingship, the first verdict of innocence and the offer of Barabbas, the flogging, the second verdict and the 'Here is the man,' the question about origin and authority, and the final sentence. The shuttle is the story's irony in physical form. The one who holds power has no peace, and the one in chains is the only person in the story who is calm.

The chapter is also woven like a sandwich. Peter's first denial, verses 15 to 18, opens the scene, then the camera cuts to Jesus before Annas, verses 19 to 24, and only then returns to Peter for the second and third denials, verses 25 to 27. The device sets Jesus' steady confession next to Peter's collapse. When Jesus is asked about His disciples and His teaching, He answers openly. When Peter is asked about being His disciple, he says 'I am not.'

The frame is deliberately theological. The chapter begins with the arrest party falling at an 'I am He,' and it ends with a crowd choosing a bandit. Between them John adds three notes saying that the events happen 'to fulfill the word,' verses 9 and 32, and that the high priest had unknowingly foretold Jesus' death, verse 14. John also leaves out what the other Gospels include: the agony in Gethsemane and the full hearing before the Sanhedrin. He gives instead what no one else records, the interview with Annas and the long private conversation with Pilate, because he wants the reader to see a king and not a victim.
context.historical:
The Kidron is the narrow ravine between the temple mount and the Mount of Olives. John's Greek calls it a winter stream, one that runs when the rains come. It carries an echo of another night of betrayal. When David fled Jerusalem before his son Absalom, he crossed the Kidron weeping and went up the Mount of Olives with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 30, and was told that his trusted counselor Ahithophel was among the conspirators, 2 Samuel 15:31. John does not say this, but a first-century Jewish reader would have felt the pattern: a king crossing the Kidron on the night he is betrayed by one close to him.

The arresting force is large. 'A band of soldiers' translates a Greek word, speira, that normally means a Roman cohort, and the 'commander' of verse 12 is the officer whose title means leader of a thousand, a tribune. Taken at face value, Roman troops stood alongside the temple officers sent by the chief priests and Pharisees. That means Pilate was involved from the beginning, which makes sense of the way the Roman governor is able to receive Jesus before dawn. Pilate was the prefect of Judea, and he normally lived at Caesarea on the coast, coming to Jerusalem at the great feasts to keep order. The Roman historian Tacitus says Christ was executed under Pilate, which agrees with the Gospels.

Annas had been high priest earlier and retained influence, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office that year, verse 13. The Jewish leaders refused to enter the Praetorium so that they would not be defiled and be unable to eat the Passover, verse 28. This is the part of the narrative that has caused debate about the Gospel's timing, as the debates below discuss. When they say 'We are not permitted to execute anyone,' verse 31, they are acknowledging a limit under Roman rule. Whatever the exact rules about capital cases, John explains the significance: it ensured that Jesus would die the way He had said, 'lifted up,' 12:32 to 33, which means Roman crucifixion and not stoning. The outcome Barabbas received is the custom of an amnesty at the feast, and the man released was a bandit, a word John uses elsewhere for violent robbers, 10:1.
context.canonical:
The arrest scene links back to the great statements of divine identity. 'I am He' is the form of speech God uses of Himself in Isaiah. In the Greek Old Testament the LORD says 'that you may know and believe Me and understand that I am He,' Isaiah 43:10, with the same words that Jesus speaks in John 18:5 and 6. John has already used the formula at 8:24, 8:28, 8:58 and 13:19, so it has a history in the Gospel, and here it becomes the sentence that knocks armed men to the ground.

The cup of verse 11 is a major Old Testament image of God's judgment. Jeremiah is told to take the cup of the wine of wrath and make the nations drink, Jeremiah 25:15 and 16. Psalm 75:8 speaks of a cup in the hand of the LORD that the wicked drink down to the dregs. Isaiah 51:17 says Jerusalem has drained the cup of His fury, and Revelation 14:10 describes the one who drinks the wine of God's anger. That cup is what Jesus is about to drink. In Gethsemane in the other Gospels He asks that it might pass, Luke 22:42, and in John He says only 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?'

The kingship scene echoes the kingdom promises of Psalm 2 and Daniel 7. In Daniel one like a son of man receives 'dominion, glory, and kingship,' Daniel 7:14, and Psalm 2:6 to 9 shows the Lord's King installed on Zion. Jesus' kingdom is the fulfilment of those promises, but it does not come by the means the world expects. Paul looks back to this moment when he tells Timothy that Christ Jesus 'made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate,' 1 Timothy 6:13. In Revelation 19:11 to 16 the same Jesus returns as 'Faithful and True,' a King who judges with righteousness. Finally, Peter's denial by the fire is answered in 21:9 to 17, where Jesus builds another charcoal fire on the shore and asks Peter three times if he loves Him, restoring what was broken here.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote this account so that his readers would see who was really in control. Every character in the chapter thinks they are acting: Judas leads, the soldiers seize, Annas questions, Peter swings a sword, Pilate decides. Yet Jesus is the one who steps forward, asks the question, names the terms of His own arrest, and sends His disciples away safe. The narrator repeatedly makes the point that events fit the word Jesus had spoken, verses 9 and 32, and the prophecy of Caiaphas, verse 14. He wants believers who suffer to know that the cross was not a loss of control. It was a self-giving carried out under the Father's purpose.

He also wants readers to see two kinds of failure and two kinds of answer. Peter fails by fear, and the Gospel later restores him. The crowd and its leaders fail by choosing: they prefer a violent man, and they call Caesar their only king. Pilate fails by evasion. He sees that Jesus is innocent, asks 'What is truth?' and does not wait for an answer. John uses the three figures as a mirror. A reader who thinks of himself as neutral in front of Jesus is, in this chapter, standing where Pilate stands. The question being asked of everyone in the story is whether they belong to the truth and will listen to His voice, verse 37.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is narrative, and most of it records what others do. Peter's use of the sword, verse 10, is reported and corrected. The denials are reported and later forgiven. The arrest, the slap, the trial and the choice of Barabbas are recorded as evil done to the Son and used by God, not as models. John expects readers to learn from the contrasts. What is prescriptive, if anything, lies in Jesus' own words and conduct. He says His kingdom is not of this world and that His servants do not fight, verse 36. That does not forbid every use of force by civil authority, which Paul says is given by God, Romans 13:1. It does mean the church does not advance Christ's kingdom by the sword, and that believers should not take up arms to defend the gospel.

Jesus' answer to the officer, 'If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong,' verse 23, shows a way of responding to abuse: truthfully, without retaliation, and without silence about what is true. Peter later says Jesus did not retaliate when abused and entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23, and holds this up as a pattern for suffering believers. The fall of Peter is descriptive: it does not excuse denial, but it shows that failure is not the end for those who belong to Jesus, as chapter 21 will show.

debates.question: Why do the soldiers fall back at 'I am He'?

views.label: A simple identification, with the fall explained by awe
views.case: In the Greek the words are a plain answer to the question, and the same words are used by the blind man in 9:9. The retreat is the reaction of a crowd in front of a calm man who knows what is coming and has taken command. The effect is natural and the narrator adds nothing about the divine name.

views.label: An echo of the divine name
views.case: The phrase is the same form used in Isaiah 43:10 and in John's earlier sayings in 8:24, 8:28 and 8:58, where an 'I am' without a predicate claims divine identity. The writer notes that Judas stood there with them and that they fell. The fall is a sign of the weight of the name, and the hearer was meant to recognize it.

views.label: Both levels together
views.case: John often writes with two layers. The words work as an ordinary answer, 'I am the man you want,' and carry the larger claim. The soldiers do not know the second layer, but the reader does, and the narrator wants the reader to see that those who come to arrest Him are powerless unless He allows it.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is chosen, the scene shows that Jesus yields only willingly. He says later that no one takes His life from Him, 10:18, and the arrest is the first public proof.

debates.question: How does John's Passover timing fit with the other Gospels?

views.label: John puts the crucifixion before the Passover meal
views.case: The leaders avoid defilement so that they can 'eat the Passover,' verse 28, and 19:14 calls the day the Preparation for the Passover. On this reading Jesus died as the lambs were being slain, and the meal in the upper room was a meal held a day earlier, in anticipation. It fits the theme of Jesus as the Passover Lamb.

views.label: 'Passover' covers the whole feast
views.case: The term can refer to the festival offerings eaten on the days of the feast, and not only the first evening meal. The leaders could have been concerned about the meals during the festival week. The Last Supper was then the regular Passover meal, and John's Preparation day is the Friday before the Sabbath.

views.label: Different calendars were in use
views.case: Some propose that different groups in first-century Judaism reckoned the feast on different days, so that Jesus and the leaders could both have been observing the feast correctly under separate reckonings. The evidence is debated.

debates.bearing: Every view agrees that the story is set at Passover and that John wants readers to see the lamb. The text does not require settling the calendar to see that.

debates.question: What does 'My kingdom is not of this world' mean for politics?

views.label: A kingdom of a different origin, which still touches this world
views.case: The Greek says the kingdom is not 'from' this world, which describes its source and not where it operates. Christ's rule is real over this world but does not derive its authority or its methods from it. It advances by witness to the truth, verse 37.

views.label: A purely spiritual kingdom with no political bearing
views.case: Some read the sentence to mean Christ has no concern with the state or public life. His servants do not fight, and the kingdom concerns the inner life and the church alone.

views.label: A kingdom that judges every worldly kingdom
views.case: Others read the verse as a challenge to all earthly claims. Jesus' answer to Pilate is that real authority is given from above, 19:11, which relativizes every ruler, and the early Christians went to their deaths rather than say 'Caesar is Lord' in the way the empire demanded.

debates.bearing: The text shows that Jesus is a king and denies that He is a rival to Caesar by force. How that works out in public life is a matter for wisdom, but the church is never to use violence to advance its Lord's rule.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase at the centre of the arrest is ego eimi, 'I am,' with no object. John's translators often supply 'He' to make it a natural English reply, and the BSB does so, but the Greek has only the two words, the first-person pronoun and the verb 'to be.' The same pair stands behind the Greek Old Testament's wording of Isaiah 43:10 and 41:4, where the LORD says 'I am He,' and it appears throughout the Gospel without a predicate, in 8:24, 8:28, 8:58 and 13:19. In verses 5, 6 and 8 Jesus uses it three times, which gives the scene a solemn rhythm. When the arresting party 'drew back and fell to the ground,' they went eis ta opiso, backward, and the second word, chamai, is 'to the ground.' The action is a reeling away from the speaker, not a bow.

The sharpest contrast comes in Peter's answers, verses 17 and 25. When the servant girl asks 'Aren't you also one of this man's disciples?' Peter says 'I am not,' ouk eimi, the exact negation of Jesus' words. John sets the two side by side: Jesus says 'I am,' and Peter, a few yards away, says 'I am not.' It is a verbal echo that no translation can sound as sharply as the Greek. The place of the denial is also given a small detail. The fire is an anthrakia, a charcoal fire, a word that the New Testament uses only here and in 21:9, so the reader who reaches the shore at the end of the Gospel will recognize the fire where Peter was restored.

The cup in verse 11 is poterion. In the Old Testament, as in the verses mentioned above from Jeremiah, Isaiah and the Psalms, the cup stands for the portion God gives, most often His wrath. The Gospel does not say what is in it, but the sentence 'the cup the Father has given Me' places the origin with the Father, and the verb 'drink' marks it as something received in full. John uses the definite 'the cup,' as though it is a known thing.

The word basileia, kingdom or kingship, appears in verse 36 three times. The key preposition is ek, 'from' or 'out of': 'My kingdom is not ek this world.' It speaks of source. The adverb 'now' in the last clause, nyn de, is logical and not a time marker: 'but as it is, my kingdom is not from here.' The word hyperetai, 'servants' or 'officers,' is the same word used for the temple police in verse 3, so Jesus says that if His kingdom were from this world His own officers would fight, as the temple's do. Pilate's 'Then You are a king!' is a question as much as a statement, and Jesus' reply, 'You say that I am a king,' is a form that neither denies nor flatly affirms what Pilate means by the word. He then restates the truth in His own terms: He was born for this, and He came to testify to the truth. The verb martyreo, 'testify,' is a legal word that belongs in a courtroom, and the setting turns the trial around so that the prisoner is the witness.

Finally, the word for truth, aletheia, has a rich background in John. It is not only accuracy but reliability and reality, what is solid beneath appearances. In 1:17 it came through Jesus Christ, and in 14:6 He says He is the truth. When Pilate asks 'What is truth?' he stands face to face with the answer. The last word of the chapter, 'insurrectionist,' translates lestes, a word for a bandit or violent robber, which John used at 10:1 and 10:8 for those who come to steal the sheep. The crowd chooses the kind of person Jesus had warned about.

typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah, the Psalms and Isaiah picture the cup of God's wrath that sinners must drink, Jeremiah 25:15 to 16, Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17. Jesus says the Father has given Him that cup and that He will drink it. The correspondence is of the portion of judgment taken. The escalation is that the one who drinks is innocent and drinks on behalf of others, so that Isaiah 51:22 can promise that the cup will be taken from the hand of the people, and Revelation 14:10 shows those who refuse the Lamb having to drink it themselves. The type falls short because Old Testament cups were drunk by guilty nations; this cup is drunk by the sinless Son, and Peter says He bore sins in His body, 1 Peter 2:24.

typology.type: The garden across the Kidron, John 18:1
typology.fulfillment: David crossed the Kidron on the night of betrayal by a close counselor, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 31. Jesus crosses the same ravine into a garden, and a trusted disciple betrays Him. The correspondence is of a king driven out of the city by treachery. The escalation is that David fled to save his life and later returned in triumph, while Jesus goes to give His life and returns in resurrection. The garden also recalls Eden, where the first Adam disobeyed in a garden, Genesis 3:6. John mentions the garden three times, here, in 18:26 and in 19:41, so that the burial and the new creation morning at the garden tomb in 20:15 follow the same place. The type falls short because David was a flawed king who fled a deserved rebellion, while Jesus was sinless.

The crowd demands the release of a guilty man and the death of the innocent one. The name Barabbas means son of the father in Aramaic, and he is a bandit. The correspondence to the scapegoat and sin offering of Leviticus 16 is not stated by John, so the link is an inference and should be held lightly. The pattern of substitution fits the wider testimony that Christ died for the ungodly, Romans 5:6 to 8, and that the innocent Servant bore the sin of many, Isaiah 53:12. The escalation is that Barabbas is freed by a crowd's vote while believers are freed by God's grace. The picture falls short because Barabbas does not know why he is free, and the believer is called to know the One who took his place.

typology.type: The silent lamb before accusers, Isaiah 53:7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant is oppressed and afflicted, yet 'He did not open His mouth,' led like a lamb to the slaughter. John does not quote the verse, but the picture is close: Jesus answers questions, but He does not defend Himself against the charges, and in 19:9 He gives Pilate no answer at all. The correspondence is of the Servant taken away by oppression and judgment, Isaiah 53:8. The escalation is that the silence is not weakness. In John Jesus speaks fully when speaking serves the truth, 18:20 and 36 to 37, and is silent when it would not. The type falls short because the lamb in Isaiah is passive, while John shows the Lamb in command of the whole event.

study.christ:
John's picture of Jesus in this chapter is of a sovereign who walks into His own arrest. The other Gospels show Him praying in agony; John, who has already given the prayer of chapter 17 and the troubled soul of 12:27, shows the outcome. 'Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon Him, stepped forward,' verse 4. The one who sees everything ahead moves toward it. He is not discovered; He identifies Himself. He is not seized; He negotiates the terms: 'let these men go,' verse 8. The Gospel explains that this fulfilled His own word, 'I have not lost one of those You have given Me,' verse 9, quoting from 17:12 as though His own sentence were Scripture. The shepherd lays down His life so that the sheep go free, 10:11 and 15.

The cup shows His obedience. Peter strikes with a sword and Jesus tells him to put it away. In Matthew's account He adds that He could ask the Father for more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:53. John's version, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?', turns the matter into filial obedience. He does not drink because He is forced, but because the Father gave it and the Son receives it. Hebrews 12:2 says He endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him.'

Before Annas and Pilate He is the faithful witness. He says He has spoken openly and said nothing in secret, verse 20, and that He was born to testify to the truth, verse 37. This ties back to 1:17, that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, and 14:6, that He is the truth. Paul remembers that He 'made the good confession' before Pilate, 1 Timothy 6:13. He is not the world's idea of a king, since He has no army and no political programme, but He is a king all the same, for whom 'everyone who belongs to the truth' is a subject. The prophets expected such a ruler, humble and riding on a donkey, Zechariah 9:9, and the crowd cried 'Blessed is the King of Israel' in 12:13. Here He stands in front of a Roman governor, and the title is truer than Pilate knows.

A word of caution. John does not say that Barabbas is a type of the sinner as an allegory, and the link between the name Barabbas and the substitution we find in the gospel is a fair application and not an exegetical claim. What is firmly in the text is the contrast: a man guilty of violence is let go and an innocent man is sent to the cross, and the Gospel has already told us why, 11:50 to 52. In Christ the one who dies instead is also the King, and the exchange is voluntary on His side.
study.god:
The chapter shows God's sovereignty working through the worst of human actions without making them any less culpable. The betrayal, the arrest, the denial, the trial and the crowd's cry all happen by human choices. Yet John adds, three times, that these things take place so that a word spoken beforehand would be fulfilled, verses 9, 14 and 32. Caiaphas says 'it would be better if one man died for the people,' and John explains in 11:51 that he was prophesying without knowing it. Luke later has the early church say that Herod and Pilate and the nations did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27 and 28. The picture is not of a God who stands by while evil triumphs and then salvages the situation. It is of a God whose plan is carried out through the choices of people who are fully responsible, and whose Son walks into it willingly.

The chapter also shows the Father and Son in agreement of will. 'The cup the Father has given Me' is language of a gift and a task. This is no tug of war between a wrathful Father and a reluctant Son. The Father gives, the Son drinks, and the Gospel has already shown that the Son and the Father are one, 10:30, and that the Father loves the Son because He lays down His life, 10:17. The wrath in the cup is real, as the Old Testament passages say, but the One who bears it does so as an act of the Father's love and His own.

God's truthfulness shapes the whole scene. The Father is the God who keeps His word, and Jesus is the one who speaks it. His promise that none of His own would be lost, 6:39 and 17:12, is kept literally in the garden, since the soldiers must let the disciples go. God's care for His people is shown in the smallest detail, and it is not undone by Peter's failure. Jesus had told Peter beforehand that he would deny Him, 13:38, and had prayed for him that his faith would not fail, Luke 22:32. The denial happens as foretold, and so does the restoration.

Finally, the kingdom is God's, and it comes in God's way. Pilate has authority, but Jesus says later that it is given from above, 19:11. God does not need swords, and His servants do not use them. His kingdom advances by testimony to the truth. Worship, in turn, is shaped by this. The Father is seeking worshipers who worship in spirit and truth, 4:23 and 24, and this chapter shows the King whose truth they worship. To belong to Him is to listen to His voice, and the humility of the King is part of what we praise.

crossReferences.note: In the prayer Jesus says that He protected those the Father gave Him and not one was lost except the son of destruction. John 18:9 quotes it as 'the word He had spoken.' The arrest scene shows the promise kept in the garden, and it places Jesus' words on the level of Scripture.

No one takes His life; He lays it down of His own accord, and He received this charge from the Father. The calm of the arrest is this principle in action. It explains why the armed party can do nothing until He steps forward and gives Himself up.

'That you may know and believe Me and understand that I am He.' The Greek form behind this is the one Jesus uses at the arrest. It shows that the words he speaks are the words of the LORD about Himself, which is why men with weapons are driven to the ground.

Jerusalem has drunk the cup of the LORD's fury to the dregs. This is one of the Old Testament places that stand behind the cup of John 18:11. Isaiah then promises in 51:22 that the cup will be taken from the hand of the people, which the Son's drinking makes possible.

In Gethsemane Jesus says 'Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.' John does not record the prayer, but his statement 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' is the conclusion of the same struggle.

King David crosses the Kidron Valley weeping on the night he is betrayed by his own circle. The detail John gives, that Jesus crossed the Kidron, makes the reader hear the pattern of the rejected and betrayed king, and sets Jesus as the true son of David.

Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people than that the nation perish, and John says he was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God. John 18:14 recalls this to show God's purpose behind the high priest's scheming.

Jesus warns that Satan has asked to sift the disciples, says He has prayed for Simon that his faith will not fail, and tells him he will deny Him three times. The denials in John 18 happen as predicted, and so does the prayer that his faith would be restored.

The risen Jesus has a charcoal fire on the shore and asks Peter three times if he loves Him. The same rare word for the fire as in 18:18 places Peter again beside a fire, this time to be restored. The three denials are met by three questions and three commissions.

The Servant is oppressed and afflicted, yet He does not open His mouth. Jesus before His accusers is close to this picture, and in 19:9 gives Pilate no answer. The passage also speaks of a Servant cut off for the transgression of the people, which the cross will fulfil.

Paul says Christ Jesus made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate. It confirms that the exchange in John 18:33 to 38 was remembered by the early church as a model of faithful witness, which Timothy is told to imitate.

The rider on the white horse is called Faithful and True, and with righteousness He judges. The King who stood bound before Pilate is revealed as the one who will judge the nations. The kingdom 'not of this world' will come into this world in power.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden and a command, and with a man and a woman who listened to another voice, Genesis 3:1 to 6. Their failure turned the world into a place where truth was contested, where people hid, and where kings ruled by force. John 18 takes up the same story. In another garden, a man stands in the place of Adam, and the question put to him is again whether he will listen to the Father's voice. Where Adam hid, Jesus steps forward. Where the first couple blamed each other, Jesus takes the whole weight on Himself and sends His friends away. The garden in which Adam was driven out is answered by a garden in which the last Adam goes willingly to death, and by 19:41 and 20:15 the story will end in a garden again.

The chapter also gathers what the Old Testament said about kings. Israel had asked for a king like the nations, 1 Samuel 8:5, and it got rulers who relied on force and failed. The prophets promised a king who would reign in righteousness, Isaiah 9:6 and 7, and a ruler who would come humble and riding a donkey, Zechariah 9:9. Jesus is that king, and when He is asked about His kingdom He describes it by its source and its method. It is from another place and it advances by truth. That is the answer to the long failure of Israel's monarchy, and it is the reason the New Testament can say that all who belong to the truth hear His voice.

Peter's denial belongs to the same story of human failure. The man who swore that he would lay down his life, 13:37, does not, and the one who laid down His life does. The covenant people who had been promised that they would be a kingdom of priests turn at the decisive moment to say 'We have no king but Caesar,' 19:15. The point is not that Israel is worse than others. The Gospel shows that every person, every nation and every institution fails when it meets Jesus. This is why the cross is necessary.

The story runs on. The cup that Jesus drinks is the cup that stood over the nations in the prophets, and Revelation shows those who refuse the Lamb drinking it, 14:10. Because He drank it, His people do not. The one who stood before Pilate will return as Faithful and True, Revelation 19:11, and His kingdom, which in this chapter is not from this world, will be the kingdom of the world, Revelation 11:15. The truth that Pilate asked about and walked away from will be seen as it is. In the new creation, the voice that men armed with torches could not withstand is heard by all who belong to it, and every person is either standing in that truth or has no place.

quiz.q: What happens when Jesus answers the arresting party with I am He?

options.text: They draw back and fall to the ground, a flash of His divine majesty.
options.note: Verse 6 shows the momentary display of majesty behind the words.

options.text: They fall back briefly and then flee in terror.
options.note: They do draw back and fall down, but they do not flee; they proceed with the arrest Jesus permits.

options.text: They laugh and mock Him.
options.note: They fall to the ground, awed, not mocking at this point.

options.text: They are momentarily overpowered by His word.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific detail that they drew back and fell to the ground.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell Peter to put away his sword?

options.text: Because He has resolved to drink the cup the Father has given Him.
options.note: Verse 11 grounds His restraint in His willing obedience to the Father's cup.

options.text: Because He is afraid of the soldiers.
options.note: He acts in sovereign resolve, not fear.

options.text: Because violence would embarrass His movement.
options.note: The real reason is His purpose to drink the cup, not concern about appearances.

options.text: Because He does not want His disciples harmed.
options.note: He does protect His disciples, but the stated reason for stopping the sword is His resolve to drink the cup.

quiz.q: How does Jesus describe His kingdom to Pilate?

options.text: It is not of this world; if it were, His servants would fight.
options.note: Verse 36 defines His kingdom as not sourced in or spread by worldly force.

options.text: It is a political kingdom to overthrow Rome.
options.note: Many expected exactly this, but Jesus denies it; His kingdom is not of this world and His servants do not fight.

options.text: It does not really exist at all.
options.note: He affirms He is a King with a real kingdom, just not of this world.

options.text: It is a reign that does not come by force.
options.note: True, but it omits the key phrase, that His kingdom is not of this world.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say He came into the world to do?

options.text: To testify to the truth, so that everyone who belongs to the truth hears His voice.
options.note: Verse 37 defines His mission as bearing witness to the truth.

options.text: To raise an army and seize the throne.
options.note: His kingdom is not of this world; He came to bear witness to the truth.

options.text: To establish an earthly reign of truth and justice.
options.note: His kingdom is bound up with the truth, but He came to bear witness to the truth, not to set up an earthly reign.

options.text: To reveal the truth to the world.
options.note: True, but it omits that those who belong to the truth hear His voice, the mark of His subjects.

quiz.q: Whom does the crowd choose when Pilate offers to release Jesus?

options.text: Barabbas, an insurrectionist, rather than Jesus.
options.note: Verse 40 records the choice of the violent Barabbas over Jesus.

options.text: They ask for Jesus to be released.
options.note: They demand Barabbas, not Jesus.

options.text: They reluctantly let Pilate make the choice.
options.note: They do not leave it to Pilate; they actively shout for Barabbas over Jesus.

options.text: A violent man instead of the King of truth.
options.note: True and pointed, but it does not name Barabbas, the specific choice the text records.

questions: Even at His arrest Jesus was in complete command, laying down His life freely. How does it change your view of the cross to see Jesus as the willing giver, not the helpless victim?
Jesus resolved to drink the cup the Father gave Him. What cup of hardship is God asking you to accept from His hand, trusting His purpose in it?
Peter denied Jesus by a fire while Jesus boldly confessed the truth. Where are you tempted to quietly distance yourself from Christ to stay comfortable?
Jesus' kingdom is not advanced by force but by truth. How does that reshape the way you think you should defend and spread His cause?
The crowd chose Barabbas over the King of truth. Where do you see the world, or your own heart, still preferring lesser things to Christ?

translationNotes.note: I have not lost one of those You have given Me recalls Jesus' words in John 6:39 and 17:12; His protection of the disciples at His arrest fulfills His own promise.
The cup the Father has given Me draws on the Old Testament image of the cup of God's wrath, which Jesus willingly drinks for His people.
The kind of death He was going to die refers to crucifixion; because the Jews could not execute, Jesus would die by the Roman method He had foretold in John 12:32-33.
Barabbas was an insurrectionist; his release in place of the innocent Jesus vividly pictures the substitution at the heart of the gospel.
